newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIA WEEK AHEAD-Currency contagion batters Asia.
newsitem.headline: ASIA WEEK AHEAD-Currency contagion batters Asia.

text.p: Peristent turmoil in Asia's currency markets is expected to depress already weak sentiment in stock markets throughout the region, with a number of currencies seeking direction while central bank policy remains unclear.
The outlook for the Singapore dollar, the Indonesian rupiah, Malaysian ringgit and the Thai baht would remain volatile after Friday's roller-coaster currency market session, traders said.

The Singapore dollar, the rupiah and the ringgit all hit new lows while central banks appeared to steer clear of the fray, raising questions about changing monetary policy in a region known for its bloc of U.S.-dollar linked exchange rates.
The persistence of the contagion was reported to be a source of concern at the International Monetary Fund.
Hong Kong and Bombay were considered safe haven stock markets, while the worst appeared to be over in the Philippines following its effective devaluation of the peso two weeks ago.

TOKYO - The Tokyo stock market's benchmark index is likely to struggle for direction after the three-day weekend, but brokers said that a handful of stocks led by high technology issues were expected to be strong.
"Investors, especially foreigners, will probably continue to seek issues based on global standards," Nobuhiro Kaneda, general manager at Daiwa Securities.
On Friday, the Nikkei 225 shed 269.93 points or 1.32 percent to finish at 20,249.32, gaining about 400 points in the course of a week. The financial markets will be closed on Monday.

HONG KONG - More volatile trade with a downward bias is expected in the week ahead, with investor attention split between Wall Street and the local banking sector in the run-up to reporting season, brokers said.

"We may track Wall Street next week, although the focus will also be on the banking sector," said Lino Delgado, associate director at Amsteel Securities. "Liquidity is still very high so we could have more volatile trading."
The Hang Seng Index dipped sharply in late Friday trade to close down 135.89 points, or 0.87 percent, at 15,570.40.
Over the week, the index gained 2.27 percent and set a new intra-day high of 15,783.27 on Thursday.

SINGAPORE - Investors will be watching out for continued movements in regional currencies. The Singapore dollar fell to an intraday 30-month low on Friday, and will be closely watched in the coming week with some dealers forecasting a slide to 1.50 to the U.S. dollar from Friday's level of 1.46.
Singapore's June non-oil export data due for release on Monday would also influence direction. An expected rise of 6.3-percent year-on-year would be considered supportive.
"If it doesn't come up to expectations, you could see a sell-off," said a dealer with a local securities house.
KUALA LUMPUR - A continuing slide on the ringgit would keep investors away from the Kuala Lumpur share market, even though prices are at their lowest levels since January 1996.
"A downtrend has already developed, with 1,000 becoming a stiff resistance," said Faez Khairuddin, head of research at SJ Securities.

The Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks closed 16.06 points or 0.60 percent lower from Friday a week ago. On Friday the index ended at 1,001.55, down 2.54 points or 0.25 percent from Thursday's close.
JAKARTA - Jakarta stocks are seen steady in the coming week with investors expected to buy after profit-taking last week but weakness in the rupiah would weigh on sentiment.
The rupiah sank to a new low on Friday.
On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed at 724.00 points, against last week's close of 723.42 points. The index was up 0.58 points, or 0.08 percent, on the week.
MANILA - Follow-through buying in Philippine shares is expected next week as investors look forward to sliding interest rates and a stabilising peso, brokers said.
"So long as the Central Bank keeps on bringing down interest rates and the peso continues to consolidate, we will see more buying," said Raul Ruiz at Sun Hung Kai Securities.
Traders expect the index to test resistance at 2,700.

The main index surged on Friday closing 52.57 points, or 2.01 percent, higher at 2,672.95 points. But over the week the index shed 28.19 points, or 1.04 percent, from 2,701.14 points the previous Friday.

TAIWAN - Taiwan share prices are expected to follow their recent bull runs and test new highs next week, but brokers said they expected a minor consolidation of bellwether electronics which have risen more than 14 percent in the past week.
Investors were expected to shift some of their gains from electronics to other major sectors, including heavy financials and plastics, brokers said.

"Electronics' downturn actually is healthy for the market because the sector has absorbed funds which would have been pegged to other shares," said Lin Long-hsien, assistant manager of the United Securities.

Brokers said the sizzling of the benchmark stock index to above the resistance at 9,600 point level on Friday has boosted investors' confidence, as reflected in the 71.90 point- or 0.74 percent gain on Saturday.
The index closed another seven-year high at 9,749.30 points, the highest level since April 12, 1990.
"With investors diversifying their investments, we expect the index to continue its uptrend next week," George Hou, fund manager of Jardine Fleming, said.
But he did not expect the index to surge past the 10,000 points due to technical and psychological pressure.
"The stock index should hover between 9,700 and 9,900 points," he said.
SEOUL - Seoul stocks are expected to slide in the coming week as troubles at the Kia Group hammer shares of Kia companies and financial firms, brokers said.
"Kia's problems will weigh on the market throughout next week," said Na Min-ho, a broker at Daishin Securities.
"The index would test 720 next week," said Kim Choon-kwon, a broker at Daewoo Securities. Brokers said small shares would be in demand in rotational buying despite overall depression.
The composite stock index ended at 742.15 on Saturday, down 25,12 points or 3.27 percent from 767.27 last Saturday.
SYDNEY - Australian shares are seen little changed near term as traders focus on key inflation data, due Wednesday, that may help satisfy the market's craving for another interest rate cut.
The All Ordinaries index closed at 2,684.2, up 0.5 percent on the day and down 0.6 percent on the week.
Miners ensured a firmer finish to the week.
"It looks okay but really I can't see much happening until we get the inflation figures," said a dealer at a Sydney-based investment bank.
WELLINGTON - A weaker currency and rising interest rates will dampen the outlook for New Zealand shares in the coming week, dealers said.
The NZ Stock Exchange's Top 40 index shed 60 points on the week to finish at 2,457.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are seen weaker in the coming week after posting a record weekly fall on political instability, brokers said.
India's fragile minority coalition faces a crisis with some partners threatening to quit the government.
Bombay's top 30-share index posted its biggest week-to-week fall this year, tumbling 197.17 points, or five percent, to end Friday at 4,124.81.
DHAKA - Positive remarks by the new Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) chief may restore investors' confidence next week following the resignation of SEC chairman Harunur Rashid.
The Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) benchmark index lost 45.76 points at 1,002.26 in the week to Thursday.
